HEADLINE: A weekend away at Stokes' beach pad
INTRO: Honestly, do we have to join the Abbott cabinet to score an invite to Kerry and Christine Stokes' beachside mansion in Broome?
TEXT:
Honestly, do we have to join the Abbott cabinet to score an invite to Kerry and Christine Stokes' beachside mansion in Broome?

A week ago we read that Prime Minister Tony Abbott and his chief of staff Peta Credlin were there last Saturday for an "intimate dinner".

And now we see on the Register of Members' Interests that Foreign Minister Julie Bishop was there at the same time the year before.

Long ago, while we weren't paying attention, Bishop declared complimentary flights from Perth to Broome to Sydney from the Stokes, as well as accommodation in Broome from August 14 to 17 in 2014.

It's not a bad investment of an Abbott cabinet minister's time considering the billionaire's power out west.

As well as the Seven TV network, Stokes owns the state's dominant paper, The West Australian - both worth having onside ahead of the byelection for the West Australian seat of Canning on September 19.

HEADLINE: Michael Thawley and the Abbott doctrine
INTRO: We tend to err on the side of Owen Harries when it comes to Australian involvement in American adventures in armed foreign policy.
TEXT:
We tend to err on the side of Owen Harries when it comes to Australian involvement in American adventures in armed foreign policy.

Our instincts say, how about we don't? Not that our opinion matters a jot on this as, off we go again, for another trip to the Middle East.

So who decided this time?

The accounts so far have stressed the role of PM Tony Abbott and our man in Washington, Kim "Bomber" Beazley.

But what of the role of Abbott's bureaucrat in chief, Michael Thawley?

We've mentioned before that back in 2003, when Thawley was Australia's ambassador in Washington, he turned up on Rupert Murdoch's Fox News to announce to Saddam Hussein (presumably a Fox subscriber): "Listen, mate, you are now at the end of the road. Destroy your biological and chemical weapons or face the consequences."

So it seems to us a stretch to assume Thawley's been pouring cold water on this latest exercise.

HEADLINE: Macquarie Group gets its Elizabeth Broderick on
INTRO: Here's a thought: in the near future Macquarie Group, the millionaire factory itself, could have a female chief executive and a female chair. High five, Elizabeth Broderick!
TEXT:
Here's a thought: in the near future Macquarie Group, the millionaire factory itself, could have a female chief executive and a female chair. High five, Elizabeth Broderick!

For years now the head of the mighty investment bank's funds business Shemara Wikramanayake has been touted as the favoured internal candidate to replace chief executive Nicholas Moore.

Despite Moore's new Sydney Opera House chair duties, he is still expected to hang around for a while yet.

The next big move is expected to be 74-year-old chairman Kevin McCann. It was expected that Kevin and fellow Mac director Gordon Cairns were going to reprise their Origin shuffle - that is, Cairns would, after a period of stewardship from the wise old man, inherit the keys to the kingdom.

But that was before Cairns, the happiest Scot we have ever met, took over the retail DIY job that is Woolworths.

As Cairns has acknowledged, his new gig is going to take up a bit of time - even with his supreme powers of mindfulness.

Which brings us back to Macquarie.

Not surprisingly, the bank's board is not short of talent. And its four female directors are not just there to make up the numbers.

The quartet are Diane Grady, Patricia Cross, Mary Reemst and, for what it's worth our tip to replace McCann if Macquarie exercises the Broderick option, Nicola Wakefield Evans.

HEADLINE: To new Fairfax Media chairman Nick Falloon!
INTRO: Staying with boards, Fairfax Media will farewell our chairman of six years Roger Corbett at drinks on Monday night at our Sydney HQ in Pyrmont.
TEXT:
Staying with boards, Fairfax Media will farewell our chairman of six years Roger Corbett at drinks on Monday night at our Sydney HQ in Pyrmont.

And we will also toast our new chairman, Nick Falloon, who all agree is a man with a great CV, a sharp mind and is devilishly handsome to boot - or so say more than a few of our Fin Review colleagues.

We also hear he's the guy you have to butter up to get a raise around here. Chairman Falloon, welcome.

HEADLINE: Bart: the man who became the face of Australian racing
INTRO: Obituary Bart Cummings globalised Australian horse racing, even though he didn't like all the consequences, writes Fiona Carruthers.
TEXT:
Obituary Bart Cummings globalised Australian horse racing, even though he didn't like all the consequences, writes Fiona Carruthers.

The irony would not have been lost on Bart. The King of Cups passed away only hours after the official start of Victoria's 2015 spring racing season - marked each year by the first group 1 race of spring, the Memsie Stakes at Caulfield.

With prizemoney totalling more than $58.7 million spread over 64 days of premium racing, the Victorian spring racing carnival's clear headline race is the Melbourne Cup, the richest handicap in the world - worth $6.2 million this year, with $3.6 million of that going to the winner of the gruelling 3200-metre race - the race Cummings won an unprecedented 12 times.

Before his death at Princes Farm, on Sydney's north-western outskirts in the early hours of Sunday, Cummings and grandson James were working towards ensuring their 10-year-old New Zealand-bred gelding, Precedence, qualified to run this year in what will be the horse's fifth Melbourne Cup.

"Hopefully that will still happen," says racing media personality Caroline Searcy. "This is a dynasty that's by no means over."

With the running of the 155th Melbourne Cup looming on November 3, the industry is plagued by more than its usual controversies at this time of year. A number of high-profile trainers - including Black Caviar's trainer Peter Moody, Melbourne Cup-winning trainer Mark Kavanagh and Danny O'Brien - continue to fight doping allegations after some of their horses returned samples containing cobalt over the permitted threshold.

The ongoing TV wars over vision rights continue. And the industry is fighting to stave off mining taking over huge chunks of the nation's thoroughbred nursery, NSW's Hunter Valley.

Now, the industry has to deal with the death of the man who came to define the elusive glory of the Melbourne Cup on the world stage. Cummings also was no stranger to controversy in his long career. In racing's finest tradition, he dealt with doping allegations, faced near financial ruin, and a very public falling out with his horse trainer son, Anthony.

"It wasn't always easy, but he won everything," says Les Carlyon, the Melbourne-based writer and author of The Master: A Personal Portrait of Bart Cummings. "He won staying races, he won Golden Slipper sprints for two-year-olds; he won more Newmarket Handicaps - a six furlong sprint - than he did Melbourne Cups. He won 13 Australian Cups. And the list goes on."

Much like the race he dominated since his first win with Light Fingers in 1965, Cummings will be best remembered for his staying power across six decades.

"With Bart, the Melbourne Cup becomes not about a horse, but a man, simply because he won 12," says Carlyon.

Victoria Racing Club chairman Michael Burn hailed Cummings's record as "peerless". "Most trainers dream of winning a group 1 race; Bart won 268," he says. "At Flemington alone he registered an astonishing 83 group 1 victories."

The boy from Adelaide, born in 1927 to father Jim, who was also a racehorse trainer, had his first taste of "the race that stops a nation" when he attended the Cup in 1950, aged 23, as strapper to the winner, Comic Court, trained by Jim.

By the time the first foreign raider was successful in the Cup - in the form of Irish horse Vintage Crop - Cummings had won nine Cups - with Light Fingers in 1965, Galilee (1966), Red Handed (1967), Think Big (1974 and 75), Gold and Black (1977), Hyperno (1979), Kingston Rule (1990) and New Zealand mare Let's Elope (1991).

By the early 1990s, when the Melbourne Cup was lagging and spectator numbers were down, Cummings was as philosophical as anyone that the race needed something new.

His staggering dominance of the race, his loud suits, brash manner and rapier wit - not to mention the big bets that handicap races attract from punters like his mate and financial backer Tan Chin Nam - helped put the race on the world stage.

Ever the wheeler and dealer with the eye on the main chance, Cummings was, however, cagey about the arrival of the so-called "foreign raiders", wary they would take over a great Australian tradition that should be the domain of local horses given it is limited to just 24 runners each year.

When Vintage Crop landed in Melbourne three weeks before the 1993 Cup, Cummings snorted: "they might as well run it at [Royal] Ascot." He decreed the gangly chestnut stayer that had just won the coveted Irish St Leger could not possibly travel halfway around the world, acclimatise and win the toughest 3200-metre flat race in the world. Vintage Crop proved the King wrong.

After that Cummings and other trainers campaigned for the VRC to invite just a handful of select international runners each year, much in the same way Australian horses must be invited to race in the Japan Cup. The campaign eventually fizzled out and last year half the field were foreign horses flown into Australia specifically for the Melbourne Cup.

"I think it was Bart being Bart in that he always liked to tease and provoke," Carlyon reflects. "At one stage, he thought the foreign horses might really take it over - then he realised later, no they wouldn't."

Carlyon points out that "in the end, he proved it didn't matter because he beat them with Saintly" in 1996, a horse bred and owned by Cummings and Tan Chin Nam. "There were some prominent internationals in that Cup, including the Irish horse Oscar Schindler," says Carlyon.

Cummings won again in 1999 with the rags to riches horse, Rogan Josh. And in 2008, Viewed won by a breath, over foreign raider Bauer, trained by the great Luca Cumani. "Bart got quite excited about the foreigners," says Carlyon. "He knew it was good for the race - good for business. And he liked that, in the end, he beat them."

Last year, the online racing journal bloodstock.com.au announced a few days out from the 154th running of the Melbourne Cup that "the build-up to the Melbourne Cup is complete with the arrival of Bart Cummings in town for Australia's biggest race".

This year, come Tuesday, November 3, the Melbourne Cup's greatest shining light will be on the track in spirit.

Bart Cummings, 87, is survived by his wife Valmae, children Margaret, Sharon, Anthony and Anne Marie, along with 14 grandchildren, including Anthony's son James, who was in partnership with his grandfather - and one grandchild, James's daughter.

Their mare, Sultry Feeling, won at Rosehill in Sydney on Saturday.

Cummings died early on Sunday morning, surrounded by his family at Princes Farm.

HEADLINE: McKibbin says climate target at 'high end'
INTRO: The Prime Minister's hand-picked economic modeller has rejected claims by the Climate Change Authority that Australia is not pulling its weight in global climate change efforts.
TEXT:
The Prime Minister's hand-picked economic modeller has rejected claims by the Climate Change Authority that Australia is not pulling its weight in global climate change efforts.

Warwick McKibbin, an internationally recognised economic modeller, writes in an opinion piece published in today's The Australian Financial Review that "to argue that Australia is not making a large contribution to the overall effort for Paris is incorrect".

This contradicts a statement two weeks ago by Bernie Fraser, the Labor-appointed chairman of the Climate Change Authority, that the Abbott government is shirking the task of tackling climate change because its emissions reduction target is near the bottom of pledges by rich countries.

"Australia's target ... when compared to other countries in terms of economic costs, is at the high end of the commitments made by all countries for Paris," writes Professor McKibbin, head of the Centre for Applied Macroeconomic Analysis at Australian National University's Crawford School of Public Policy.

"The size of the global target is important for climate change but an equal allocation across countries is not a measure of effort. It is a political measure used for political purposes."

Professor McKibbin, who is also a senior non-resident scholar at the Brookings Institution in Washington, accuses Mr Fraser and others focusing only on emission targets of "playing politics" with climate.

He writes that this approach reduces the prospects for a successful outcome from the United Nations-sponsored Paris talks in December.

"Until the economic costs relative to the environmental benefits are at the core of the global response, there will not be an effective global agreement," Professor McKibbin writes.

His modelling found that the proportionate reduction in Australian economic output would be three to six times higher than for the US and Europe - even though its emissions pledge is less ambitious - because natural resources play such a big role. Real wages and consumption would also fall, as the nation invested in low-emissions energy technology and the cost of energy rose.

But the estimates are uncertain; access to international emissions permits at current low prices could almost halve the cost to the economy. Lower technology costs could cut the cost by a third.

The mining industry prefers Professor McKibbin's approach. "Australia's emissions are higher than some other nations, not because we are bad people, but because we provide other nations with protein and fibre to feed their population, and minerals and energy to power their economies and build their essential infrastructure," said Brendan Pearson, chief executive of the Minerals Council of Australia.

The Abbott government wants to abolish the Climate Change Authority, which was created by Labor, but has been blocked by the Senate.

Professor McKibbin modelled the impact on the Australian economy of global emissions reductions pledged for the Paris talks by other countries, and the impact of Australian emissions cuts in two separate reports.

Under the Abbott government's emissions reduction target of at least 26 per cent from 2005 levels by 2030, gross domestic product would be 0.6 per cent lower than if there were no target - a bit under $20 billion - or a cumulative $200 billion over the 15 years to 2030.

Professor McKibbin also modelled a 45 per cent emissions cut - within the 40-to-60-per-cent range sought by the Climate Change Authority - and found it would lower GDP by 1 per cent.

Consumption and real wages would be hit even harder. The modelling shows consumption falling 0.8 per cent under the government's target and 1.4 per cent under a 45 per cent target.

Real wages would be 1.5 per cent lower under the government's target than if there were no target, and 2.7 per cent lower under a 45 per cent target.

By contrast, the US target of a 37 per cent emissions reduction by 2030 would only cut that country's GDP by 0.1 per cent by 2030; Europe's target of a 34 per cent emissions cut by 2030 would cut its GDP by 0.2 per cent, and Japan's 22 per cent emissions pledge would only cut its GDP by 0.02 per cent by 2030.

Only China with a 0.4 per cent hit to GDP, and Canada, with a hit of 0.8 per cent, face comparable sacrifices.

HEADLINE: Fairfax's Corbett retires, slams Canberra's 'reform holiday'
INTRO: Retiring Fairfax Media chairman Roger Corbett says the nation's political environment has created a "reform holiday", which has left media ownership rules in the dark ages, and threatens to undermine Australians' standard of living.
TEXT:
Retiring Fairfax Media chairman Roger Corbett says the nation's political environment has created a "reform holiday", which has left media ownership rules in the dark ages, and threatens to undermine Australians' standard of living.

Mr Corbett, who is also a Reserve Bank board member, said a hostile Senate meant Prime Minister Tony Abbott had lost the ability to govern; he called for an early double-dissolution election to break the impasse.

"The position we are in politically is untenable," Mr Corbett said in a wide-ranging interview to mark his retirement from the Fairfax Media board after 12 years, including almost six as chairman.

"If I was Tony Abbott that's exactly what I would do, because he is in a position where he can't govern. We've got a reform holiday in this country, and we've got a reform holiday because we have got a government that while it's got a mandate in the House of Representatives, the electorate has not given it a mandate in the Senate."

Mr Corbett singled out the government's failure to overhaul media ownership rules, which prohibit Fairfax from merging with any of the metropolitan TV networks, as an example of the policy vacuum in Canberra that was stifling economic growth. Mr Corbett, 72, also confirmed he would be stepping down from the boards of the Reserve Bank and US retail giant Wal-Mart in December. He will remain a consultant to Wal-Mart.

Speaking to The Australian Financial Review ahead of his last day chairing Fairfax, Mr Corbett said Fairfax Media was in a strong position following a period of upheaval after the digital revolution decimated newspaper classified advertising streams.

However, he said he was worried by the government's failure to bring media laws into the digital age, which was a hurdle to consolidation opportunities, while favouring Rupert Murdoch's News Corp and Kerry Stokes' media assets.

Mr Abbott last month resisted Communications Minister Malcolm Turnbull's efforts to abolish rules that limit the number of media platforms a company can own in a single market, following lobbying by Mr Stokes and News Corp. "He [Mr Abbott] is elected to make decisions that are in the best interests of the population of Australia, and very clearly the media rules are absolutely totally redundant and as his own minister says we should move to change them," Mr Corbett said.

A controversial deal between News Corp's pay television venture Foxtel and Ten Network Holdings has put the media laws back in the spotlight. Fairfax Media, which publishes The Australian Financial Review, has asked the competition watchdog to look at Foxtel's acquisition of a 15 per cent stake in Ten, which also counts Lachlan Murdoch as an 8.5 per cent shareholder. "What has now happened is that Rupert Murdoch, who I have the highest regard for ... but one of his overall characteristics is whenever he spots weakness, throughout the whole of his career ... if there is a commercial opportunity, exploits it," Mr Corbett said.

"This is only the first stage, I believe, and he [has] completely got around the media rules and he's got around them because of the political situation that we are currently in."

Mr Corbett's last day as chairman of Fairfax Media was Friday, making way for former Ten Network Holdings executive chairman Nick Falloon to take the job. Mr Corbett, a former Woolworths chief executive whose first job was in the loading docks at Grace Bros, was chairman during a period of enormous upheaval for newspapers globally. In 2010, he ousted former Fairfax chief executive Brian McCarthy, who later accused the board of lacking media experience, and installed Greg Hywood. Mr Corbett praised Mr Hywood but said Mr McCarthy's time running the company was "an absolute disaster".

A defining moment of his chairmanship was standing up to mining magnate and major shareholder Gina Rinehart in 2012. Mrs Rinehart, who has since sold her 14.99 per cent stake in the company, had demanded two board seats but refused to sign Fairfax's charter of editorial independence.

"She chose to attack me personally in the press," Mr Corbett recalls. "You notice that I didn't respond and she was entitled to my respect as a major shareholder and I treated her with every courtesy. But we are fiercely of the view that our editorial independence is absolutely important and it was in a sense under some challenge here," Mr Corbett said, adding it was disappointing that she made it personal.

The outspoken Mr Corbett, who was attacked for strident criticism of former prime minister Kevin Rudd and fell out with former health minister Jillian Skinner, has had his fair share of public stoushes, but joked that criticism only hurt if it was warranted.

"If mud thrown at you has some truth in it then it has two characteristics: it both hurts and sticks. If it's got no truth in it ... it doesn't hurt you personally because you know it isn't true."

Fairfax's share price has fallen from about $1.70 when Mr Corbett became chairman to 84¢ on Friday. But it has made a sharp recovery from a low of 36¢ in October 2012, helped by a sweeping cost restructuring. Fairfax, which also owns The Sydney Morning Herald and The Age, beat market forecasts with its full-year results this month and flagged strong growth at the property portal Domain.

When asked to comment on Mr Corbett's retirement, Fairfax Media chief Mr Hywood said: "His biggest achievement is his leadership of the company through a very trying time. He's a man driven by values, and those values were of press freedom, and that really came to the fore during that time."

Mr Corbett said he joined the board in 2003 "at the end of - you might call it - a recovery period". David Kirk replaced Fred Hilmer as chief executive in 2005, which Mr Corbett said was the start of a period when the impact of digital was becoming obvious and the company bought into online portals Trade Me, RSVP and Stayz.

While Mr Corbett said Fairfax managed to retain its dominant position in real estate, he described the decision not to buy carsales.com as an "unfortunate mistake". He rejected suggestions the company should have acquired SEEK, saying it was never available to buy.

Asked if Fairfax could have moved earlier on digital media, he said: "The answer is yes, but you can't judge yesterday in today's mindset. It was unchartered. The biggest part was when we took the papers away from the paper people and gave it to [former Fairfax Metro Media chief] Jack Matthews."

"[That] caused us to make a lot more progress than our competitors have made around the world, so I am quite pleased with that strategy."

Mr Corbett praised NSW Premier Mike Baird, but said Australia needed political leaders federally who had the gravitas of past prime ministers such as Bob Hawke, Paul Keating or John Howard. He warned that time was running out to fix problems such as Australia's industrial relations system, but he also believed the market turmoil caused by fears about slowing Chinese growth had been overdone. "Our standard of living in this country will deteriorate, and I think you could argue our standard of living is deteriorating."

Mr Corbett, who presided over seven years of double-digit earnings growth at Woolworths, would not comment on the supermarket group's poor recent performance, but confirmed he had not been asked to become its new chairman.

Michael.smith@fairfaxmedia.com.au

HEADLINE: GST to pay for income tax cuts
INTRO: The Abbott government has rekindled the prospect of paying for its promised income tax cuts by increasing the GST, earning it the support of the NSW government but the condemnation of the federal opposition.
TEXT:
The Abbott government has rekindled the prospect of paying for its promised income tax cuts by increasing the GST, earning it the support of the NSW government but the condemnation of the federal opposition.

A week after Treasurer Joe Hockey flagged using spending cuts to fund the return of bracket creep, federal Finance Minister Mathias Cormann said any income tax cuts would be part of a broader reform package, potentially involving an increase in the goods and services tax, that would be taken to the election.

"That is our objective: to take to the next election a tax reform package," Senator Cormann told Sky News.

He said spending cuts alone would not be enough to fund a tax cut.

"Right now we are focused on getting spending growth under control. That gives us some room, but obviously if we want to raise less revenue from one tax source you have to take from other areas and that is the conversation we are currently having."

He said there was a "conversation to be had" with the community on changes to the GST.

"The conversation is ongoing; I am not going to pre-empt where we are going to land in terms of our reform package that we take to the next election, but clearly there is a conversation to be had," he said.

"We have always said in relation to the GST that we would want to see a broad community consensus and a broad political consensus in the context of any such reform, but certainly the conversation so far has been encouraging."

Participants at last week's National Reform Summit were divided over the GST. Despite those present urging that all options should be kept on the table regarding tax reforms, unions and welfare groups were generally opposed to any increase, while business groups supported an increase, but more to fund a cut in company income tax rather than personal income tax.

Former Treasury secretary Martin Parkinson told the summit it was indisputable that Australia's high reliance on company tax and personal income tax weighed on productivity and hence growth.

The NSW Liberal government and South Australian Labor government have been calling for the GST rate to be increased from 10 per cent to 15 per cent and for the extra revenue to be spent on the growing cost to state governments of public health.

They also argue there should be compensation in the form of income tax cuts and welfare increases for those earning under $100,000, which is more than 90 per cent of income earners.

Mr Baird told The Australian Financial Review on Sunday that Senator Cormann's comments were consistent with this position.

"I welcome the Finance Minister's comments. They reflect the NSW position - that an increase in GST, with targeted tax cuts to quarantine the majority of families from the effect, is the best way to secure the future of our health services," he said

"This solution addresses the cumulative deficits looming for the Commonwealth and the states, while improving the overall competitiveness of the Australian economy."

While the Abbott government has previously said that any increase to the GST would have to be offset by other tax cuts to ensure there was no overall increase in the tax take, Senator Cormann said there was still room to increase the amount of tax revenue collected as a proportion of the economy to help fund tax cuts. The tax-to-GDP ratio is currently just over 22 per cent, well below the 23.9 per cent peak reached during the Howard years.

The latest Intergenerational Report predicts that ratio to be reached by the end of this decade by when at least bracket creep would have to be returned.

Labor, which has yet to release its full tax policy, has also left open increasing the amount tax collected as a proportion of GDP.

"The tax-to-GDP ratio is going up under the current government and Australia needs a tax to GDP ratio which is adequate to fund important community services, not a dollar more, not a dollar less," shadow treasurer Chris Bowen said in April.

On Sunday, however, Mr Bowen said federal Labor remained emphatically opposed to any increase to the rate or base of the GST.

"Tony Abbott promised 33 separate times not to change the GST, prior to the last election," he said.

"Tony Abbott also promised to lower taxes and instead we've got the highest tax burden since the Howard government and it's rising each and every budget year.

"Now Tony Abbott and Joe Hockey have a plan to increase taxes further through the GST."

Previously, the government has ruled out touching the GST without the approval of every state and territory.

But with Victoria and Queensland opposed, the Abbott government has started shifting its language, speaking instead of a broad consensus.

HEADLINE: WA chilling as big miners cut $20b spending
INTRO: A dramatic $20 billion cut in operational spending by the nation's three biggest iron ore miners is chilling a West Australian economy already under stress from falling investment in resources-related construction.
TEXT:
A dramatic $20 billion cut in operational spending by the nation's three biggest iron ore miners is chilling a West Australian economy already under stress from falling investment in resources-related construction.

Analysis by The Australian Financial Review reveals that since 2012, BHP Billiton, Rio Tinto and Fortescue Metals Group have cut the amount they spend on extracting resources by $US14.3 billion ($19.9 billion).

While this figure includes BHP and Rio's global operations, the majority of the cuts have been generated from their West Australian iron ore operations.

This excludes massive cuts to capital expenditure. With laser-like precision the miners are tightening the cost screws beyond cutting staff and salaries. They're cutting meals served on flights to remote mine sites, pulling biscuits from the tea rooms and reducing the number of uniforms issued to staff.

Rio Tinto swapped leaving safety glasses and gloves in a box for staff to take for a vending machine. It has cut use by staff - who must swipe their employee card to access the free safety gear - by between 15 per cent and 20 per cent.

Rio Tinto iron ore managing director Andrew Harding said the move, which makes staff accountable for consumption, saves Rio millions of dollars each year. The cuts in turn place pressure on suppliers.

Wesfarmers' industrial and safety business supplies safety glasses to miners, which are among more than 200,000 various industrial and safety products it sells.

It has felt the impact of the downturn, responding by shedding about 10 per of its workforce in the past few years as part of restructuring its operations. It may sell safety glasses but big drops in use by miners including Rio Tinto does not necessarily equate to similar volume drops for Wesfarmers, according to Wesfarmers industrial and safety managing director Olivier Chretien.

Wesfarmers supplies the vending machines. Because the vending machines can only use its particular range of safety glasses and gloves it forces the mine site to buy in its products rather than that of a competitor. "There is a lot more volume reduction [for the customer]," Mr Chretien said. "For us, it means all our products get sold. We get better compliance with our contract so for us while it is a bit of a drop [in volume] it is not as much as that."

Mr Chretien said the business has also increased direct sourcing from Chinese factories to help cut its costs and improve its own supply chain.

Rio Tinto's cost-cutting drive has been so successful that it has increased its target this year from $US750 million to $US1 billion, taking total cuts since 2012 to $US5.8 billion.

BHP will also keep cutting after stripping out $US7.8 billion from its global operations - including iron ore and coal - while Fortescue wants to drive down costs by $US1.4 billion this year, taking total cuts to $US3 billion since 2012. About a third of the cost cuts by Fortescue in the June quarter came from "procurement initiatives". Those initiatives it said are only half complete and shaved off $US2 per tonne from its cost base.

The miners are increasingly centralising buying, triggering a reduction in the number of suppliers that provide everything from safety protection to mine-site equipment and services.

Wesfarmers' industrial business is not the only one being buffeted by cooling economic winds.

Commercial property group JLL estimates 65,700 square metres of office space has been dumped by the mining industry and a further 58,500 square metres has been quit by businesses servicing the mining industry, such as engineering and consulting firms.

That is roughly enough space to fill Perth's tallest office tower, Central Park, two times over.

Perth's central business district office vacancy rate is now the highest in the country, reaching 17.4 per cent in the June quarter, the since January 1996. A glaring example of the downturn is the vacant top four floors at Central Park. For the first time since the building was built in 1992 that the top four floors are for lease.

Yet this prime CBD real estate has been empty for about two years, triggering a $4 million refurbishment by the building owners, which also spent $11 million upgrading the lifts.

JLL regional director office leasing David Evans said he is in advanced negotiations for three of the four vacant floors to a professional business services group.

Mr Evans said while tenants were enjoying strong incentives to take up space he is confident the current downturn will not be as bad as the early 1990s, when the vacancy rate shot up to 32 per cent.

"The fundamentals of the WA economy are still very sound," he said. "There is a much broader and diverse economy. We have strong retail, agriculture and finance sectors."

Savills director Graham Postma said rent for A-grade office space has dropped about 40 per cent. "It has hit a point that it may not have bottomed but it is close to it," Mr Postma said. "There has been a flight to quality."

CBRE senior director Andrew Denny agreed the market was "not as severe as the early 1990s recession".

Mr Denny said rest of the market beyond mining and mining services was doing well and there was demand from professional services groups.

HEADLINE: Pressure builds on Labor over 'dud' China trade deal
INTRO: Three major industry groups have launched a campaign to generate public support for the China trade deal as Jacqui Lambie became the fourth senator to voice concerns about the deal, putting more pressure on Labor.
TEXT:
Three major industry groups have launched a campaign to generate public support for the China trade deal as Jacqui Lambie became the fourth senator to voice concerns about the deal, putting more pressure on Labor.

The National Farmers' Federation, the Minerals Council of Australia and the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry are urging Parliament to ratify the deal before the year's end to lock in benefits from tariff cuts, via a national TV advertising campaign.

The debate heated up at the weekend as unions stepped up demands on Labor to change the body of the agreement or the side deals and Liberals argued union campaigns would have no impact on the Canning byelection.

Earlier in August, senators John Madigan, Nick Xenophon, Ricky Muir, and Glenn Lazarus, and the Greens voted for a motion calling on the government to either change or abandon the China-Australia Free Trade Agreement but Senator Lambie did not vote.

Now a spokesman for Senator Lambie said if the deal and the yet-to-be-tabled legislation failed to allay her concerns about threats to Australian jobs, she would be open to voting against it. "All options are open to her."

On the subject of lobbying from business groups, unions and Labor, she was also concerned over ISDS clauses, worried associated litigation would take funds away from areas such as health and veterans' affairs.

The spokesman warned the government over its approach to negotiations with crossbenchers, saying if it wanted to "get on the front foot, they can learn to communicate with rather than ambush crossbenchers".

Finance Minister Mathias Cormann, has argued the claims in the union campaign against components of the free trade deal will not hit Canning, the site of a key coming byelection.

He said people in Canning and in WA were "very conscious of the importance for this deal" since a lot of growth in Western Australian hinged on Chinese demand for resources.

"People in Western Australia, perhaps more so than other parts of Australia, very well understand the importance of the trade relationship with China," he said.

On Sunday, ACTU head Dave Oliver told the ABC the deal was a "dud".

Asked how it could be changed, Mr Oliver said: "I think there's a number of ways. You've got the actual body of the agreement itself, you've got the side deals that are being done.

"My message to Labor, the crossbenchers and the Greens, is that they should not be passing this trade deal unless we can get this issue adequately addressed."

Labor's trade spokeswoman Penny Wong has said Labor was up for the agreement but was asking the government to address the safeguards issues in order to pass it through Parliament.

Instead of changes to the deal itself, Labor is likely to push for amendments to the the Migration Act to force Chinese companies to test the local job market before bringing in their own workforce on projects worth $150 million and over.

On Sunday, Opposition Leader Bill Shorten said Labor maintained its concerns over skills assessments and labour market testing.

"Well, let's see whether the government's prepared to negotiate. We're going to put up sensible amendments ... We want to make sure that Australians are not going to lose work," he said.

Going harder, Labor senator Sam Dastyari, said "there are bits of this agreement we want to try and improve", and government claims that the agreement with China could not be changed were "baloney".

Trade Minister Andrew Robb wants the relevant legislation passed by December to allow the deal to take effect from January.
